text:
New research reveals we can squeeze giant artificial intelligence systems into small models without losing their smarts. 

Training huge computer models works great for learning complex patterns from massive data [P3_p1_c03]. But running these giant systems for everyday users is often too slow and expensive [P3_p1_c02, P3_p1_c03]. 

To solve this, scientists use a new technique called distillation [P3_p1_c03, P3_p2_c04]. Think of it like insects that have a larval form optimized for extracting energy and nutrients from the environment, and a completely different adult form optimized for travel and reproduction [P3_p1_c03]. We train a big, cumbersome model to extract knowledge [P3_p1_c03]. Then, we transfer that learned knowledge into a smaller, lean model that is more suitable for deployment and ready for public use [P3_p1_c02, P3_p1_c03]. 

Instead of just looking at final right or wrong answers, the small model learns from rich hints about subtle probabilities [P3_p2_c04, P3_p5_c02]. For instance, it learns the valuable information defined by ratios of very small probabilities, such as how often a handwritten two might slightly resemble a three or a seven [P3_p2_c04]. 

This matters because it makes top-tier technology fast and cheap enough for a large number of users [P3_p1_c02, P3_p1_c03]. The results are striking. More than 80% of the accuracy gains achieved by a massive group of ten separate models successfully transfer into a single, streamlined distilled model [P3_p5_c02]. Researchers also significantly improved the acoustic model of a heavily used commercial system using this exact approach [P3_p1_c02].
